message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe.

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Common isotope** | ^1H (protium) – 99.98 % natural abundance |
| **Other stable isotopes** | ^2H (deuterium, 0.02 %) and ^3H (tritium, radioactive, ~10⁻¹⁰ %) |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average weighted by natural isotopic composition) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Second ionization energy** | 24.587 eV (2375 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative, meaning energy is released when an electron is added) |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.44 K) at 1 atm |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) at 1 atm |
| **Density** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C, 1 atm (lowest among all elements) |
| **Molar volume** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ (ideal gas at STP) |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas |
| **Bonding** | Forms covalent bonds; diatomic molecules (H₂) are the most common form. Can also form hydrides with metals or nonmetals. |
| **Acidity/Basicity** | Acts as a weak acid (forming H₃O⁺ in water) and a very weak base (forming OH⁻). In its ionic form, H⁺ is a proton. |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive; reacts with oxygen to form water (exothermic), with halogens to form hydrogen halides, with metals to form metal hydrides. |
| **Uses** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), rocket propellant, industrial hydrogenation, ammonia synthesis (Haber process), medical imaging (MRI contrast agents using deuterated compounds), laboratory standard gas. |
| **Safety** | Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air (1–4 % H₂ in air). Requires careful handling and proper ventilation. |

---

### Quick Facts

* **Lightest element** – only one proton and one electron in its ground state.
* **Most abundant element** – makes up about 75 % of the visible universe’s baryonic mass.
* **Isotopic significance** – Deuterium is used in nuclear fusion research; tritium is used in nuclear weapons and fusion reactors.
* **Chemical behavior** – Despite being a noble gas‑like element (no valence electrons), it readily forms covalent bonds due to its high electronegativity relative to other gases.

Feel free to ask if you’d like more details on any specific property!
